This page goes with **Chapter 7, Roman Numerals** of Robert Hutchinson's open textbook
[*Music Theory for the 21st-Century Classroom*](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/RomanNumeralChordSymbols.html). Read each section
there first; the book is the reference for the symbols used here. It assumes [Chapter 6, Triads](triads.qmd).

Every drill grades each answer and has **Settings** (your teacher's link may set them; you can change them, and **Back to the link's
settings** undoes it). They are also on the [Theory Drills](theory-drills.qmd) page. Typing is **case-sensitive**, because the case is
the quality: *V* is a major chord, *v* a minor one.

## 7.1 Roman numeral symbols

A Roman numeral names a chord by the scale degree of its root, so the same pattern looks the same in every key. Capitals are major (*I*),
small numerals minor (*ii*), a small numeral with ° diminished (*vii°*), a capital with + augmented (*III+*). The key is written before
a colon: a capital letter for major (*G:*), a small one for minor (*f:*). Until figured bass (Chapter 16), the book shows an inversion by
naming the chord member in the bass: *V/3rd* is V with its third in the bass, *iv/5th* is iv with its fifth in the bass.
[Read 7.1](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/RomanNumeralChordSymbols.html) ·
[musictheory.net: Roman Numeral Analysis](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons/44) ·
[Open Music Theory: Roman Numerals](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/roman-numerals/)

The drills accept *6* for /3rd and *64* for /5th as well, if you already know figured bass.

## 7.2 Diatonic chords in major

Build a triad on every note of a major scale, using only the notes of the key, and the qualities always come out the same:
**I ii iii IV V vi vii°** (major, minor, minor, major, major, minor, diminished).
[Read 7.2](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/DiatonicChordsInMajor.html) ·
[musictheory.net: Diatonic Triads](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons/43)

<div class="drill" data-ex="rn" data-settings="mode=major&most=3&inv=root&clef=treble"></div>

The other way round: given the key and the numeral, write the chord's notes (the book's exercise 2).

## 7.3 Diatonic chords in minor

Minor has three scales (natural, harmonic, melodic), so its 6th and 7th degrees can be raised or not, and there are 13 possible diatonic
triads. The ones used most are **i ii° III iv V VI VII vii°**. **V** and **vii°** take the raised 7th (the leading tone) from harmonic minor,
so they need an accidental. **VII**, the subtonic, is built on the lowered 7th and needs none. The rarer ones (v, III+, ii, IV, ♯vi°)
are in the drill's **Chords in minor** setting.
[Read 7.3](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/DiatonicChordsInMinor.html) ·
[musictheory.net: The Minor Scales](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons/22) ·
[Open Music Theory: Minor Scales](https://viva.pressbooks.pub/openmusictheory/chapter/minor-scales/)

<div class="drill" data-ex="rn" data-settings="mode=minor&most=3&minorset=common&inv=root&clef=treble,bass"></div>

<div class="drill" data-ex="rnwrite" data-settings="mode=minor&most=4&minorset=common&inv=root"></div>

## 7.4 Cadences

A **cadence** is the harmonic arrival at the end of a phrase. The book names four:

- **Authentic (AC):** V to I.
- **Plagal (PC):** IV to I.
- **Deceptive (DC):** V to something other than I, most often vi.
- **Half (HC):** the phrase stops on V.

[Read 7.4](https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/cadences.html) ·
[musictheory.net: Phrases and Cadences](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons/55) ·
the site's own [Cadences lesson](/lessons/cadences.qmd), where the band plays each one

Name the cadence: look, listen, or both (**Show** in Settings; *Sound only* is ear training).

<div class="drill" data-ex="cadence" data-settings="mode=major&most=3&cads=AC,PC,DC,HC&show=both"></div>

## For teachers

- **Links with your settings:** open a drill's **Settings**, then **Copy a link with these settings**. Add `&lock=1` for a test, `&count=20` for a score.
- **Minor keys:** the minor-key drills follow the book's common set by default. *All 13* adds v, III+, ii, IV and ♯vi° (the book's spelling, with the sharp before vi°).
- **Answers the drills accept:** the book's /3rd and /5th, and also 6 and 64. `o` works for °, `#` for ♯.
- **Spelling:** the writing drills want the accidental the key needs. In c minor, V is G B♮ D; typing B for B♮ is right, because the natural is the plain letter.
- **Videos:** the clips use the book's YouTube links and start and end times. Each title was checked against YouTube.
- **Missing exercise:** musictheory.net has no Roman numeral exercise; its chord identification names chords by letter, not by numeral.
:::
